la:verb:dico.gloss: to say, talk, speak, utter, mention
senses: to say, talk, speak, utter, mention
to appoint, name, nominate (to an office)
to mean, speak in reference to, refer to
la:verb:dico.html:
dĭco, āvi, ātum, 1 (dixe for dixisse, Val. Ant. ap. ; DICASSIT dixerit, Paul. ex ; rather = dicaverit), v. a.
orig. the same word with 2. dīco; cf. the meaning of abdĭco and abdīco, of indĭco and indīco, dedĭco, no. II. A. al., Corss. Ausspr. 1, 380
.
To proclaim, make known. So perh. only in the foll. passage: pugnam, Lucil. ap. .—Far more freq.,
Relig. t. t., to dedicate, consecrate, devote any thing to a deity or to a deified person (for syn. cf.: dedico, consecro, inauguro).
Prop.: et me dicabo atque animam devotabo hostibus, Att. ap. : donum tibi (sc. Jovi) dicatum atque promissum,; cf.: ara condita atque dicata, (for which aram condidit dedicavitque, ); so, aram,; : capitolium, templum Jovis O. M.,: templa,: delubrum ex manubiis,: lychnuchum Apollini,: statuas Olympiae,: vehiculum,: carmen Veneri,; cf. et saep.: cygni Apollini dicati,.—
With a personal object, to consecrate, to deify (cf. dedico, no. II. A. b.): Janus geminus a Numa dicatus,: inter numina dicatus Augustus,.—
Transf., beyond the relig. sphere.
To give up, set apart, appropriate a thing to any one: recita; aurium operam tibi dico,; so, operam,; : hunc totum diem tibi,: tuum studium meae laudi,: genus (orationis) epidicticum gymnasiis et palaestrae,: librum Maecenati,; cf.: librum laudibus ptisanae,: (Deïopeam) conubio jungam stabili propriamque dicabo,; cf. the same verse, : se Crasso,; cf.: se Remis in clientelam, * : se alii civitati,to become a free denizen of it,; for which: se in aliam civitatem,fin.—*
(I. q. dedico, no. II. A.) To consecrate a thing by using it for the first time: nova signa novamque aquilam,.— Hence, dĭcātus, a, um, P. a. (acc. to no. II.), devoted, consecrated, dedicated: loca Christo dedicatissima, August. Civ. Dei, 3, 31: CONSTANTINO AETERNO AVGVSTO ARRIVS DIOTIMVS ... N. M. Q. (i. e. numini majestatique) EIVS DICATISSIMVS,.

senses: to appropriate to, devote to, assign to, set apart for

la:verb:dicto.html:
dicto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.
2. dico
,
to say often; to pronounce, declare, or assert repeatedly.
In gen. (very rare): rogarem te, ut diceres pro me tu idem, qui illis orationem dictavisses,: mercemur servum qui dictet nomina,; cf. .—Far more freq. and class.,
In partic.
To dictate to one for writing: quod non modo Tironi dictare, sed ne ipse quidem audere scribere,; b. fin.; 2, 23; ; ; ; et saep. So of the dictating of teachers (common for want of books): memini quae mihi parvo Orbilium dictare,; cf. .—
Transf. As the practice of dictating came, in the course of time, to be very general (v. Gesner upon ), dictare, since the Aug. per., acquired the signif. to express in written language, make, compose: elegidia,; so, ducentos versus,: carmina (for which, shortly before and after, scribere), : codicillos,to draw up, make,; cf. testamentum,; hence also, summas,i. e. to dispose of by will,; and in the pass.: non unus tibi rivalis dictabitur heres,appointed, designated,; so, actionem,to draw up a declaration,; and among jurists in gen.,to bring an action, go to law,; also, judicium,; —
To prescribe, recommend, order, dictate (cf. 2. dico, no. I. B. 10; in this sense the primitive of dictator, although no ante-Aug. examples occur): sportulam,: dictataque jurant Sacramenta deis, .—
Transf., of abstract subjects: ita videtur ratio dictare,; cf. : quibus sordet omne, quod natura dictavit,; so with acc., ; ; .—Hence, dictāta, ōrum, n. (acc. to no. II. A.).
Things dictated by the master to his scholars, i. e. lessons, exercises, rules, ; ; ; ; ; ; —Also, in gen.,
Precepts, rules, e. g. for gladiators, ; for mimes,.

la:noun:dica.html:
dĭca, ae, f., = δίκη, law t. t.,
a lawsuit, judicial process, action. Usually in the phrase dicam scribere (alicui) = δίκην γράφειν τινί, to bring an action against any one, ; ; ; ; : subscribere,; and stronger, impingere, to bring a heavy action against one, : e lege Rupilia sortiri dicas oportere,to select the jury by lot,.

la:noun:dicis.gloss: only in the terms dicis causā, dicis ergō, and dicis grātiā
senses: only in the terms dicis causā, dicis ergō, and dicis grātiā
la:noun:dicis.html:
dicis,
gen. [v. 2. dico], in the phrase dicis causa or gratia, orig. a jurid. t. t., meaning for the sake of judicial form; hence, in gen., for form's sake, for the sake of appearance, λόγου χάριν: ut illis aliquid nummulorum dicis causa daret,; Orell. N. cr.; ; : dicis gratia,; ; .—
Transf.: si Pontifici accidat dicis causa epulanti,; Orell. N. cr.: dicis ergo = dicis causa, P.

la:noun:dictus.html:
dictus, ūs, m.
2. dico
,
a saying, speech, Aur. Vict. epit. 14.

la:noun:dictator.html:
dictātor, ōris, m.
dicto, qs. a commander
.
A dictator, the chief magistrate in several Italian states, elected by the Romans in seasons of emergency for six months, and armed with absolute authority; formerly called Magister populi, and also Praetor Maximus,; ; ; ; ; Lydus de Magistr. 1, 36-38 et saep.; cf. Mommsen, Hist. Book I. ch. 2; 1, p. 330 N. Y. ed. Anthon's Smith's Antiq. p. 360; Kreuz. Excurs. XII. to .—The chief magistrate of other cities of Italy, ; ; ; ; ; —
Transf., of Hannibal, as chief of the Carthaginians, Column. Rostr.; cf. Cato ap. .—
Qui dictat, one who dictates,

la:verb:dicendus.gloss: which is to be said, uttered; mentioned, spoken
senses: which is to be said, uttered; mentioned, spoken
which is to be declared, stated
which is to be called, named
which is to be referred to

la:verb:dictito.html:
dictĭto, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. intens. a. [dicto], to say often or emphatically; to declare, maintain, assert repeatedly (good prose).
In gen.: non, obsecro, es, quem semper te esse dictitasti,.; cf. ; : qui ita dictitat, iis esse metuendum, etc.,; ; ; 2, 1, 8: ut Lacedaemonii suos omnes agros esse dictitarint, quos spiculo possent attingere,: Caelius profectus, ut dictitabat, ad Caesarem pervenit, as he alleged, or pretended, ; cf. and 6; Kritz.; ; ; ; —Pass. impers.: male dictitatur tibi volgo in sermonibus,there are bad rumors about you,.—*
In partic., in jurid. lang.: causas,to plead frequently,.

la:noun:dicrotum.html:
dicrŏtum, i, n. (sc. navigium), = δίκροτος (two-oared),
a galley with two banks of oars, ; fin.—Also called dicrŏta, ae, f. (sc. navis), Auct. B. Alex. 47, 2.

la:noun:dictio.gloss: a saying, speaking, speech, talk, oratory
senses: a saying, speaking, speech, talk, oratory
la:noun:dictio.html:
dictĭo, ōnis, f.
2. dico
,
a saying, speaking, uttering, delivery.
In gen.
(Good prose, for the most part only in jurid. and rhetor. lang.) Sententiae, : testimonii, i. e. the right of giving testimony, *: causae,a defending, pleading,; ; * ; : multae ovium et boum,—
Kinds of delivery, style, diction: seposuisse a ceteris dictionibus eam partem dicendi, quae, etc.,; so, oratoriae,: subitae,: et vero fuit in hoc (Crasso) popularis dictio excellens; Antonii genus dicendi multo aptius, etc.,: extemporales,: discipulorum,declamation,: saeptuosa dictione, opp. aperte dicere, Rib.— Hence,
The use of a word or phrase, a mode of expression, ; ; ; .—
A word, = verbum, vocabulum (late Lat.), —
Esp.
(Cf. dictum, B. 4.) An oracular response, prediction (rare; not in Cic.): flexa, non falsa autumare dictio Delphis solet, Pac. ap. (R); Att. ap. ; .—
The art of speaking, oratory: dictioni operam dare,.

la:noun:dicio.gloss: military or political authority, power, control, rule
senses: military or political authority, power, control, rule
la:noun:dicio.html:
dĭcĭo, ōnis (less correctly, ditio; occurs only in the
gen., dat., acc., and abl. sing., and in plur. once, ; so Hemsterhuis, Orat. p. 7.—Georges rejects the dat. sing., but v.infra; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, 514 sq.), f.
root dic-; Sanscr. dicami, point out; Gr. δείκνυμι; Lat. dico; cf.: condicio, judex
, a t. t., milit. and polit., dominion, sovereignty, authority, rule, sway, power.
Prop.: Commagenem, dicionis regiae usque ad id tempus, etc.,: Poenum quod inter Alpes Apenninumque agri sit, suae dicionis fecisse,; so,; cf.: Tyros mare dicionis suae fecit,—Dat.: regionem dicioni ejus adjecit,; cf.: subjecit dicioni suae hostes,: dicioni alicujus se permittere,; ; ; ; ; : gentem dicioni nostrae subicere,; cf. under no. II.—Acc. (very freq.): dedunt se, urbem et liberos In dicionem atque in arbitrium Thebano poplo,; so,; al.; cf.: omnia in dicionem tradere,: omnes eas civitates in dicionem potestatemque populi Romani esse redactas,; so,; ; ; : et saep.; cf.: urbes multas sub imperium populi Romani dicionemque subjunxit,; and: Ilergetes in jus dicionemque recepit,: sub populi Romani imperium dicionemque cadere,; cf.: voluntate concedere in dicionem,: in dicionem venire,; so,; et saep.: in amicitiam populi Romani dicionemque esse, (cf. on the constr. esp. Kritz ad ).—Abl. (also very freq.): sub alicujus dicione atque imperio esse,; : nationes, quae in eorum regno ac dicione sunt,; and: in parte magis quam in dicione alicujus esse,: in servitute atque in dicione alicujus teneri,; cf.: terras omni dicione tenere,; so,: dicione premere aliquos,; cf. .
Transf., beyond milit. and polit. life: auris meas dedo in dicionem tuam,: postquam res publica, in paucorum potentium jus atque dicionem concessit,: omnis gentis, etc. ... decemvirum dicioni, judicio potestatique permissa esse,; cf.: sub dicione ejus magistratus (sc. censoris),: respirare contra nutum dicionemque alicujus,: aliquem in sua potestate ac dicione tenere,: caput liberum fidei suae commissum alienae dicioni subicere, (dub. al. condicioni).

dictŭrĭo, īre,
v. desid. a., to long to say or tell (late Lat.): fortiter a se facta semper dicturiunt,; .

la:noun:dicacitas.html:
dĭcācĭtas, ātis, f.
id.
,
biting wit, raillery, banter (for syn. cf.: sal, facetiae, cavillatio, lepos, urbanitas): dicacitas sine dubio a dicendo, quod est omni generi commune, ducta est; proprie tamen significat sermonem cum risu aliquos incessentem,; cf. ; ; ;

la:noun:dictamen.html:
dictāmen, inis, n.
dicto
, late Lat. for dictum, praescriptum, praeceptum.

la:noun:dictatura.html:
dictātūra, ae, f.
id.
.
The office of a dictator, dictatorship, ; ; * ; ; fin.; ; ; et saep.—*
The work of dictating to pupils; only in a play upon the double meaning in the sentence: Sullam nescisse litteras, qui dictaturam deposuerit, Caes. ap. .

la:adj:dicax.html:
dĭcax, ācis, adj.
1. dico
,
talking sharply, satirical, sarcastic, acute, witty (class.): Demosthenes non tam dicax fuit quam facetus. Est autem illud acrioris ingenii, hoc majoris artis,; cf. ; so with facetus,; ; with venustus and urbanus, *Catull. 22, 2; with lascivus, Caelius in ; with cavillator, et saep.: Satyri,: dicax in aliquem,: argutia, et saep.—Comp., ; .—Sup., .—Adv. does not occur.
